lessons.title: Introduction and Why It Matters
lessons.body:
Foundry work is one of the most dangerous trades you can learn. Every year, thousands of workers in Africa are injured or killed in small foundries because they ignore basic safety. The risks are real: molten metal at 1200Â°C can burn through flesh in seconds, silica dust from sand moulds causes lung disease, and heavy crucibles can crush feet. But with the right precautions, you can work safely and productively.

In countries like Nigeria, Kenya, and South Africa, many foundries operate in informal settings with poor ventilation and no protective gear. A 2019 study in Nigeria found that over 70% of foundry workers had experienced at least one burn injury. Most of these accidents are preventable. This module will teach you the safety rules that keep you alive and healthy.

Why does safety matter? First, your life and limbs are irreplaceable. Second, a safe foundry is a productive foundryâaccidents stop work and cost money. Third, customers and regulators trust businesses that follow safety standards. Whether you are melting scrap aluminium in a backyard or casting bronze for art, safety must be your first thought every day.

We will cover personal protective equipment (PPE), safe handling of molten metal, ventilation, fire prevention, and emergency procedures. You will learn to identify hazards before they cause harm. Remember: no job is so urgent that you cannot take time to be safe. In the foundry, complacency kills. Let's begin.

lessons.title: Tools and Materials
lessons.body:
Safety in the foundry requires specific tools and materials. You don't need expensive imported gear; many items can be sourced locally or made by a tailor or welder. The minimum PPE for any foundry work includes: a face shield (not just safety glasses) to protect against molten metal splashes, a leather apron or heavy cotton overalls, leather gloves (gauntlet style), safety boots with steel toes, and a hard hat if working under overhead loads. In Africa, you can buy these from industrial markets like Kariobangi in Nairobi or Ladipo in Lagos. Expect to pay $30-$50 for a basic set.

For ventilation, you need a way to remove fumes and dust. A simple roof vent or open-sided shed works for small operations. For indoor work, install a fan that pulls air out. You also need a fire extinguisherâdry powder type ABCâand a bucket of dry sand to smother metal fires. Never use water on a metal fire; it causes explosions.

For handling molten metal, you need proper crucible tongs, a pouring shank, and a skimmer. These can be made by a local blacksmith. Always check for cracks before use. For first aid, keep a burns kit with clean water, sterile gauze, and burn gel. Also have a fire blanket and a designated safe area for quenching hot tools.

Other useful items: a CO2 monitor if using gas furnaces, a respirator (N95 or better) when mixing sand or grinding, and a metal bucket for dross. Keep a logbook to record incidents and near-misses. In the next lesson, we'll show you how to use these tools step by step.

lessons.title: Step by Step Method
lessons.body:
Follow these steps every time you enter the foundry. Step 1: Dress properly before you start. Put on your PPE: boots, apron, gloves, face shield, and if needed, a respirator. Never wear synthetic clothing like polyesterâit melts onto skin. Step 2: Inspect your area. Check that the floor is dry and clear of obstacles. Ensure ventilation is working. Look for any flammable materials (paper, cloth, oil) within 3 meters of the furnace and remove them.

Step 3: Prepare your tools. Lay out your tongs, skimmer, and moulds. Check crucibles for cracks or chipsâdiscard any damaged ones. Fill your quenching bucket with water and have dry sand ready. Step 4: Light the furnace. If using coke or charcoal, start with small pieces and gradually add fuel. Never use petrol or kerosene to light a furnaceâuse paper or wood shavings. For gas furnaces, check hoses for leaks with soapy water before igniting.

Step 5: Melt metal. Stay at least 1 meter away from the furnace opening when charging. Use tongs to add metal, never your hands. Watch for moistureâwet metal can cause a steam explosion. Step 6: Skim dross. Use a skimmer to remove impurities. Tap the skimmer gently on the crucible edge to shake off dross into a metal bucket. Step 7: Pour. Wear your face shield. Pour steadily and slowly into the mould. Keep the crucible close to the mould to reduce splashing. Step 8: After pouring, shut off the furnace and let it cool completely before cleaning. Step 9: Clean up. Sweep floors, dispose of dross safely, and wash your hands and face. Step 10: Record any issues. Always work with a buddy if possible. Never rush.

lessons.title: Common Mistakes and Fixes
lessons.body:
Mistake 1: Not wearing a face shield. Many beginners think safety glasses are enough. But molten metal splashes can go over glasses and burn your face. Fix: Always wear a full face shield. If you can't afford one, use a welding mask with clear lens.

Mistake 2: Pouring wet metal. Moisture on scrap metal turns to steam instantly, causing an explosion that sprays molten metal. Fix: Pre-heat all metal before charging. Keep scrap under a roof or in a dry place.

Mistake 3: Using water on a metal fire. Water reacts with molten aluminium or magnesium to produce hydrogen gas, which explodes. Fix: Keep dry sand, a CO2 extinguisher, or a fire blanket nearby. Never use water.

Mistake 4: Poor ventilation. Working in a closed room with a charcoal furnace builds up carbon monoxide, which is odourless and deadly. Fix: Work outdoors or in a shed with open sides and a roof vent. Install a CO detector if you work indoors.

Mistake 5: Loose clothing or jewellery. A dangling sleeve or necklace can catch on a crucible or get caught in a machine. Fix: Wear fitted clothing, remove rings, watches, and necklaces. Tie back long hair.

Mistake 6: Skipping maintenance. Cracked crucibles, frayed hoses, and worn gloves cause accidents. Fix: Inspect tools daily. Replace damaged items immediately. Keep a maintenance log.

Mistake 7: Working alone. If you get burned or trapped, no one can help. Fix: Always work with a buddy. If you must work alone, tell someone your schedule and check in.

Mistake 8: Ignoring burns. Even small burns can get infected. Fix: Cool a burn with clean running water for 20 minutes, cover with sterile gauze, and seek medical help if it's larger than a coin. Never apply oil or toothpaste.

Mistake 9: Not training new workers. Many accidents happen to untrained helpers. Fix: Train everyone on safety before they enter the foundry. Use this module as your guide.

lessons.title: Safety and Best Practice
lessons.body:
Safety is not a one-time lesson; it's a daily habit. Here are the best practices that professional foundries in Africa follow. First, develop a safety culture. Hold a 5-minute safety talk every morning before work. Discuss hazards, review incidents, and remind each other of rules. Second, use the hierarchy of controls: eliminate hazards where possible (e.g., use electric furnaces instead of coke), substitute safer materials, use engineering controls (ventilation), then administrative controls (rotating shifts), and finally PPE as the last line of defence.

Third, manage heat stress. Foundries are hot. Drink water every 20 minutes, even if not thirsty. Take breaks in a cool area. Watch for signs of heat exhaustion: dizziness, nausea, heavy sweating. Fourth, prevent fires. Keep a 3-meter clear zone around furnaces. Store flammable liquids in a separate shed. Use fire-resistant walls. Have a fire extinguisher within 10 meters and check it monthly.

Fifth, handle chemicals safely. Sand binders, fluxes, and degreasers can be toxic. Read labels, wear gloves and respirators, and store in sealed containers. Sixth, maintain good housekeeping. A cluttered floor causes trips and falls. Sweep daily, keep tools organized, and store materials properly. Seventh, report all incidents, even near-misses. This helps you fix problems before they cause injury.

Eighth, get first aid training. At least one person in your team should know CPR and burn care. Ninth, use lockout/tagout for maintenance. Turn off power and lock switches before repairing equipment. Tenth, respect the metal. Molten metal is unforgiving. Never joke around near a furnace. Always assume metal is hot. By following these practices, you protect yourself, your workers, and your business. Remember: safety doesn't cost, it saves.

lessons.title: Practical Exercise
lessons.body:
Now it's time to put your safety knowledge into practice. This exercise has three parts. Part 1: Conduct a hazard hunt. Walk through your foundry or workspace. Use a notebook to list every hazard you see. Examples: exposed wires, cracked crucible, oily rags near furnace, missing face shield, blocked exit. For each hazard, write a fix and a deadline. Share your list with a supervisor or mentor. Aim to fix at least three hazards within one week.

Part 2: Set up a safety station. Create a dedicated area with: a fire extinguisher (ABC dry powder), a bucket of dry sand, a first aid kit (burn gel, gauze, bandages), a fire blanket, and a logbook. Label everything clearly. Make sure everyone knows where it is. Test your fire extinguisher by checking the pressure gaugeâif it's in the red, replace it. Practice using a fire blanket by smothering a small controlled fire (in a safe outdoor area).

Part 3: Do a dry run of an emergency. With a buddy, simulate a molten metal spill. One person shouts "Spill!" and everyone follows the emergency plan: turn off furnace, evacuate to a safe distance, and if trained, use sand or extinguisher. Practice until you can do it in under 30 seconds. Also practice a burn response: cool with water for 20 minutes, cover, and seek help.

After the exercise, write a short report: what you learned, what you will change, and what supplies you need. If you lack PPE, make a plan to buy or make it. For example, a leather apron can be made from an old car seat cover. A face shield can be improvised from a clear plastic bottle and a head strap. But don't compromiseâproper gear is best. Finally, teach one other person what you learned. Safety multiplies when shared.

quiz.q: What is the minimum recommended face protection when pouring molten metal?
quiz.explanation: A full face shield protects against splashes that can go over safety glasses.

quiz.q: Why should you never use water on a molten metal fire?
options: A) It makes the fire hotter
quiz.explanation: Water reacts with molten metal to produce hydrogen gas, which can explode.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to light a coke furnace?
options: C) Use paper or wood shavings
quiz.explanation: Petrol and kerosene are highly flammable and dangerous; paper or wood shavings are safe.

quiz.q: How often should you drink water when working in a hot foundry?
quiz.explanation: Frequent water intake prevents heat stress and dehydration.

quiz.q: What should you do before charging metal into a furnace?
options: A) Heat it to remove moisture
quiz.explanation: Pre-heating removes moisture that can cause steam explosions.

quiz.q: Which type of fire extinguisher is suitable for metal fires?
quiz.explanation: ABC dry powder is safe for metal fires; water and foam can react violently.

quiz.q: What is the first step in the step-by-step method?
quiz.explanation: Putting on PPE is the first step to ensure safety before any work.

quiz.q: Why is good ventilation important in a foundry?
options: A) To keep the metal cool
B) To remove fumes and carbon monoxide
C) To make the fire burn brighter
quiz.explanation: Ventilation removes toxic fumes and prevents carbon monoxide buildup.

quiz.q: What should you do if you get a small burn?
options: C) Cool with running water for 20 minutes
quiz.explanation: Cooling with water reduces damage and infection risk; oils and toothpaste worsen burns.

quiz.q: Why is it dangerous to wear loose clothing in the foundry?
options: A) It can catch fire easily
B) It can get caught in equipment
quiz.explanation: Loose clothing can snag on crucibles or machinery, causing accidents.

quiz.q: What is a near-miss?
options: A) An accident that causes injury
B) An unplanned event that did not cause harm
quiz.explanation: Near-misses are incidents that could have caused harm but didn't; reporting them helps prevent future accidents.

quiz.q: How far should flammable materials be kept from the furnace?
quiz.explanation: A 3-meter clear zone reduces fire risk from sparks and heat.

quiz.q: What should you do before repairing a furnace?
options: A) Turn it off and lock out
C) Ask a colleague to watch
quiz.explanation: Lockout/tagout ensures the equipment cannot be started accidentally during maintenance.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT part of basic foundry PPE?
quiz.explanation: Sandals do not protect feet from molten metal or heavy objects; safety boots are required.

quiz.q: What is the correct action if you see a cracked crucible?
quiz.explanation: Cracked crucibles can fail and spill molten metal; they must be discarded.

quiz.q: Why should you work with a buddy in the foundry?
options: B) To have help in case of emergency
quiz.explanation: A buddy can call for help or provide first aid if an accident occurs.

quiz.q: What is the first thing to do in an emergency molten metal spill?
quiz.explanation: Turning off the furnace stops the source of the spill and prevents more metal from escaping.

quiz.q: How can you check a gas hose for leaks?
quiz.explanation: Soapy water bubbles indicate a leak; never use a flame to check.

quiz.q: What is the recommended minimum for a first aid kit in a foundry?
options: B) Burn gel, gauze, and bandages
quiz.explanation: Burn-specific supplies are essential for treating common foundry injuries.

quiz.q: Why is it important to report all incidents, even minor ones?
options: B) To identify and fix hazards
quiz.explanation: Reporting helps find root causes and prevent future accidents.

quiz.q: What does the hierarchy of controls prioritize first?
quiz.explanation: Elimination is the most effective control; PPE is the last line of defence.

quiz.q: What is a safe distance to keep the crucible from your body when pouring?
quiz.explanation: Keeping distance reduces the risk of burns from splashes.

quiz.q: What should you do with dross after skimming?
options: A) Throw it on the floor
B) Put it in a metal bucket
D) Leave it on the crucible
quiz.explanation: Dross is hot and can start fires; a metal bucket is safe.

quiz.q: Why is synthetic clothing dangerous in a foundry?
options: B) It melts onto skin when hot
quiz.explanation: Synthetics melt and stick to skin, causing severe burns.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to remove a crucible from the furnace?
quiz.explanation: Crucible tongs are designed to grip hot crucibles safely.

quiz.q: How often should you inspect your PPE?
quiz.explanation: Daily inspection ensures PPE is in good condition and safe to use.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a fire blanket?
quiz.explanation: Fire blankets cut off oxygen to small fires.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of heat exhaustion?
quiz.explanation: Dizziness and nausea are early signs; act quickly by cooling and hydrating.

quiz.q: What should you do if a fire starts in a crucible?
options: B) Cover with a lid or sand
quiz.explanation: Covering with a lid or sand cuts off oxygen; water causes explosions.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep the foundry floor clean?
options: B) To prevent slips and trips
quiz.explanation: A cluttered floor causes falls, especially when carrying hot metal.
